Voted to accept the "Ought Not to Pass" committee report on LD 1134, "An Act to Prohibit Males from Participating in Female Sports or Using Female Facilities," which would have barred transgender girls/women from participating in female school sports or using female facilities based on sex; accepting ONTP killed the ban (House Roll Call #481, 6/13/2025, prevailing 73-72). Voting to reject an outright competition ban is the clearest evidence available, matching stance 2 as the nearest pro-inclusion chair this record supports.

Was the primary sponsor of LD 868, 'An Act to Ensure Equity and Safety in Athletics, Restrooms, Changing Rooms and Housing at Elementary, Secondary and Postsecondary Schools,' and told the Maine Wire in July 2025 that allowing biological males to compete in girls' sports 'denies biological reality'; separately voted Nay on the motion to accept the 'Ought Not to Pass' report on the related LD 1134 (House Roll Call #481, 6/13/2025), keeping that bill alive (motion to kill it failed 73-72).

On House Roll Call No. 481 (6/13/2025, verified on the authoritative rollcall.asp page), Farrin voted Yea to accept the committee's "Ought Not to Pass" report on LD 1134, "An Act to Prohibit Males from Participating in Female Sports or Using Female Facilities." Under Maine's ONTP convention a Yea vote KILLS the bill, meaning Farrin voted against imposing a sex-based eligibility restriction on transgender athletes. This matches the stance 1 chair.

Voted Yes on 2025 Assembly Joint Resolution 102 (second consideration), a proposed constitutional amendment creating Article I, Section 27, under which no governmental entity “may not discriminate against, or grant preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration.” “Governmental entity” is defined to cover the state, its political subdivisions, the UW and Technical College Systems, every public school district, the legislature and the courts. The amendment's entire purpose is to end race- and sex-conscious government programs, which is what the most restrictive position on this scale describes: eliminating affirmative action and all race-based government programs. Recorded vote: 2025 Assembly Vote 137, 54-45.

Voted Yes on 2025 Assembly Bill 840, which directs the Public Service Commission to ensure in its rate-making orders that “no costs associated with the construction or extension of electric infrastructure that primarily serves the load of a data center are allocated to or recovered from any other customer,” and requires that any renewable energy facility primarily serving a data center be located at the data center site. The bill also mandates closed-loop cooling, annual water-use reporting to the DNR, and a reclamation bond. Those first two provisions are precisely the two clauses of this scale's second position: requiring data centers to fund their own dedicated power generation, and barring utilities from passing data center infrastructure costs through to other customers. The bill also mandates closed-loop cooling, annual water-use reporting to the DNR, and a reclamation bond. Those first two provisions are precisely the two clauses of this scale's second position: requiring data centers to fund their own dedicated power generation, and barring utilities from passing data center infrastructure costs through to other customers. Recorded vote: 2025 Assembly Vote 182, 53-44.

Booker voted NAY on S.9 (Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act) in May 2025 which would have banned transgender athletes from competing on teams matching their gender identity, reflecting full support for transgender inclusion without restrictions.

Blumenthal voted NAY on the cloture motion for S. 9 (Title IX athletics bill that would have required transgender athletes to compete based on biological sex at birth), on March 2025 vote 100. He has supported LGBTQ equality throughout his career and opposes legislation restricting transgender participation in sports.

Cantwell voted NAY on the cloture motion for S.9, the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act (Senate vote 100, March 2025), which would have required transgender athletes to compete only on teams matching their biological sex. Her consistent support for transgender non-discrimination protections reflects a position of allowing transgender athletes to compete on teams matching their gender identity.

Gallego voted NAY on cloture for S. 9 (Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act March 3 2025) opposing the bill that would require transgender athletes to compete based on biological sex assigned at birth. His vote supports allowing transgender athletes to compete on teams matching their gender identity after completing basic documentation of their transition.

Murray voted NAY on the cloture motion for S.9 (Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act) on March 3 2025 which would have required transgender athletes to compete based on biological sex. Her 100% HRC rating and consistent LGBTQ+ rights record support allowing transgender athletes to compete matching their gender identity after completing transition documentation.

Merkley voted NAY on the cloture vote for S.9 (March 2025) the bill that would have restricted transgender athletes to competing based on biological sex. He also supported gender-affirming care in federal prisons via press statement reflecting consistent support for transgender rights.

Smith voted NAY on S.9 (Senate vote 100, March 2025), which would have required transgender athletes to compete based solely on biological sex assigned at birth for Title IX compliance. Her NAY vote reflects support for transgender athletes competing on teams matching their gender identity after completing basic transition documentation.

Van Hollen voted Nay on S.9 (Feb 2025) the bill restricting Title IX compliance to biological sex at birth opposing requirements that transgender athletes compete under their birth sex; he also opposed the 2017 transgender military ban.

Moody voted Yea on cloture for S. 9 (Vote 100, February 2025), the Title IX athletics bill defining sex as 'solely based on a person's reproductive biology and genetics at birth' — which would require transgender athletes to compete on teams matching their biological sex assigned at birth. The cloture vote failed 51-45 but her vote clearly establishes her position.

Heinrich voted NAY on S.9 (March 2025) which would have required Title IX athletics compliance to be determined solely by biological sex at birth effectively banning transgender women from competing in women sports. His opposition aligns with allowing transgender athletes to compete on teams matching their gender identity after basic transition documentation.

Reed voted NAY on S. 9 (the Senate cloture vote, March 3, 2025), which would have defined sex in Title IX athletics based on biology at birth to ban transgender athletes. He supports transgender rights including opposing the Pentagon transgender ban (2019).

Klobuchar voted NAY on S.9 (Senate roll call 100, 2025), the measure to restrict transgender athletes to competing only based on biological sex assigned at birth under Title IX, joining all Democrats in opposition and signaling support for transgender athletes competing on teams matching their gender identity after basic documentation.

Hassan voted NAY on the cloture motion for S.9 the Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act (Senate vote 100 March 2025) which would have required transgender athletes to compete only on teams matching their biological sex at birth. Her consistent record supporting transgender non-discrimination protections places her at allowing transgender athletes to compete on teams matching their gender identity.

King voted Nay on the cloture motion for S.9 (Senate roll call 100, March 2025), the bill to require Title IX athletics compliance based solely on biological sex at birth — joining all Democrats in opposing restrictions on transgender athletes.

Risch voted Yea on cloture for S.9 (March 2025, Roll Call Vote 100), a bill defining sex for Title IX athletics purposes solely based on reproductive biology at birth, and co-led an amicus brief supporting Idaho and West Virginia laws prohibiting biological males from participating in women's sports under Title IX.

Murphy voted NAY on the cloture motion for S.9 (Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act) on March 3, 2025, which would have required Title IX compliance to be based on biological sex at birth; he has spoken out against policies preventing transgender youth from participating in sports.

Kennedy voted Yea on the Title IX sex-in-sports cloture amendment in March 2025 requiring that sex in athletics be determined by reproductive biology at birth. In January 2025 he co-introduced a bill with Sen. Tuberville to safeguard women's sports and protect Title IX, and wrote an op-ed in May 2024 titled Protect women's sports from transgender inclusion.

Warnock voted NAY in March 2025 on cloture for S.9, the bill that would have required transgender athletes to compete based on biological sex at birth, opposing the measure. His HRC endorsement and support for the Equality Act reflect support for transgender rights and competing on teams matching gender identity after basic transition.

Durbin voted NAY on Senate cloture vote 100 (119th Congress) on S.9 Protection of Women and Girls in Sports Act (March 2025) which would have required transgender athletes to compete based on biological sex. Opposing this bill aligns with allowing transgender athletes to compete consistent with their gender identity.

Voted Yes on 2025 Assembly Joint Resolution 102 (second consideration), a proposed constitutional amendment creating Article I, Section 27, under which no governmental entity “may not discriminate against, or grant preferential treatment to, any individual or group on the basis of race, sex, color, ethnicity, or national origin in public employment, public education, public contracting, or public administration.” “Governmental entity” is defined to cover the state, its political subdivisions, the UW and Technical College Systems, every public school district, the legislature and the courts. The amendment's entire purpose is to end race- and sex-conscious government programs, which is what the most restrictive position on this scale describes: eliminating affirmative action and all race-based government programs. Fischer opposes affirmative action in public employment and contracting and voted against the Respect for Marriage Act (2022). No strong documented position on religious freedom specifically. Whitehouse's support for LGBTQ+ protections and the Respect for Marriage Act (YEA, vote 362, 2022) suggests he prioritizes anti-discrimination protections, but his record does not show extreme positions on either strong religious autonomy or strict separation of religion from public life.

Kelly voted YEA on H.R. 8404 the Respect for Marriage Act (Senate Vote 362 Dec 2022 passed 61-36) which repeals DOMA and requires federal and state recognition of same-sex marriages with full federal benefits. He was endorsed by the HRC as a voice for equality.

Moody voted Yea on H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill reconciliation, Vote 372, July 2025) which extended the 2017 Trump tax cuts and reduced corporate and individual tax rates. She voted Nay on the Rosen Amendment providing tax relief for the middle class (Vote 190) — a Democratic alternative — favoring the Republican approach of across-the-board rate reductions rather than targeted middle-class relief.

Moody's Senate page explicitly states she focuses on 'supporting President Trump's agenda' including deregulation and economic growth. Her record shows consistent opposition to taxes, regulations, and government interference in private markets. She voted for the Big Beautiful Bill which included major business incentives and tax cuts. Her conservative deregulatory posture aligns with offering maximum incentives to attract any large employer.

Moody voted Nay on the Markey Amendment preserving Social Security's phone service (Vote 187, rejected 48-51) and voted Yea on H.R. 1 reconciliation which contained spending cuts affecting social programs. She has not called for full privatization of Social Security but her consistent vote against protecting Social Security services and support for spending cuts aligns with gradually raising the retirement age and reducing benefits for higher earners.

Moody voted Nay on an amendment to preserve Medicaid funding and prevent rural hospital closures (Vote 186, rejected 49-50), Nay on an amendment creating a point of order against Medicaid funding reductions (Vote 188), and Nay on Medicare drug pricing protection (Vote 185). She voted Yea on H.R. 1 (Vote 372) which contained significant Medicaid spending reductions. Her record aligns with partially privatizing Medicare and reducing Medicaid coverage.

OnTheIssues records Gallego as opposing Trump corporate tax cuts supporting raising estate taxes and favoring closing tax loopholes for the rich. He voted NAY on the final reconciliation bill (H.R. 1 July 2025) which extended TCJA tax cuts and voted YEA on a middle class tax relief amendment consistent with modestly increasing taxes on high earners while maintaining current rates for middle-class families.

Moody received a 0% environmental score from the League of Conservation Voters in 2025 — voting against all 35 tracked environmental measures including wind and solar credits, clean air protections, and methane fee. She voted for the Big Beautiful Bill reconciliation (Vote 372) which eliminated clean energy incentives. Her record shows consistent rejection of climate policies in favor of economic priorities.

Gallego voted YEA on S.Amdt. 2186 (March 2025) to reverse DOGE cuts to the Social Security Administration and voted NAY on the final reconciliation bill (H.R.1 July 2025) which included provisions reducing Social Security and Medicare funding. OTI records him as opposing privatization and personal retirement accounts consistent with modestly increasing benefits while raising taxes on higher earners.

Moody received a 0% LCV environmental score in 2025 and voted against clean energy investments, for reversing land management restrictions on Arctic drilling (Vote 632), and for eliminating clean energy incentives in the Big Beautiful Bill reconciliation. Her senate page states she supports maximizing Florida's energy resources and economic growth priorities over environmental restrictions.

Moody voted YES on H.R. 1 (One Big Beautiful Bill reconciliation, July 2025) which reduced childcare subsidy provisions and cut social spending broadly. Her conservative profile — law enforcement focus, pro-deregulation — aligns with reducing regulations on childcare providers and reserving limited subsidies only for the lowest-income families rather than broad public subsidies.

Moody voted against budget amendments protecting affordable housing (Vote 65, Nay on point of order against legislation increasing housing costs) and voted for the Big Beautiful Bill reconciliation which cut HUD and housing assistance programs. Her conservative profile favors reducing housing regulations and letting private developers address housing shortages over federal housing construction programs.
